title: Matplotlib: plotting with Python

spans.text: WHY USE THIS?

Matplotlib's original author was John D. Hunter. He created it to make 2D scientific plots in Python, export publication-quality figures, and embed plots in interactive applications. Simple charts take only a few commands, while the object-oriented API allows detailed control.
PURPOSE AND SETUP

A plot helps compare numbers quickly and spot trends or unusual measurements. Matplotlib and Seaborn create plots that can be shown on screen or saved to a file. Install the examples with `python -m pip install matplotlib seaborn pandas`.
RUNNABLE EXAMPLES
Example 1: plot how the temperature changes throughout the day.
QUESTION: What plot will this code create? Predict first, then run it.

spans.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

hours = [8, 10, 12, 14]
temperature = [18, 21, 24, 23]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(hours, temperature, marker='o')
ax.set(xlabel='Hour', ylabel='Temperature (C)', title='Daily temperature')
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()
A line graph titled "Daily temperature" opens.

WHICH CHART SHOULD I CHOOSE?

• `plot`: trends over time or order; a line connects points. `step`: discrete, step-like signals.
• `scatter`: relationship between two numeric variables; correlation does not prove causation.
• `bar` / `barh`: compare categories. `hist`: show a numeric distribution grouped into bins.
• `pie`: part-to-whole proportions for a few categories; many slices are hard to compare. A bar chart is often clearer for precise comparisons.
• `boxplot` / `violinplot`: compare group spread; a violin also shows distribution shape.
• `errorbar`: measurement uncertainty; `fill_between`: shade an interval or range.
• `stackplot`: cumulative parts over time; `stem`: discrete samples. Use `subplots` to separate different questions into panels.

The charts use the axes returned by `fig, ax = plt.subplots()`. `plt.show()` opens a plot in an interactive environment; servers and automated tests should use `fig.savefig('chart.png', dpi=150)` and call `plt.close(fig)` when finished. `ax.set()` adds clear titles and axis labels.
